subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you call the function in the [on start] container with a [call createBubbles] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


﻿Ask the ninja:

❓ Why does the [for index] loop run 10 times, when 9 is used as the parameter?

❓How is the [for index] loop similar to and different from the [for element] loop?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to open the tilemap (even though it’s blank) to notice the dimensions of the tilemap: 10 (columns) by 8 (rows). Prompt the ninja to make the connection between the number of tiles across 1 row (10, based on the number of columns) and how that reflects the value used in the [for index] loop to place Bubble sprites.

💡 Remind the ninja that the [for index] loop begins counting at 0. This means that the loop will run one more time than the value listed in the parameter.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by creating a single row of Bubble sprites!


Create a function called [createBubbles]. Open Loops, drag a [for index] loop inside the container, then set the loop to run from 0 to 9. 


Drag the Bubble sprite’s [set sprite to] block from the [on start] container into the [for index] loop. Add a [place sprite on top of] block then select the Bubble sprite’s name. Drag the (index) variable into the col parameter, to place one sprite in each column of row 0. Call the function in the [on start] container with a [call createBubbles] block. Call the function before the Marble and Paddle sprites are created.


The [for index] loop will start counting at 0 and count up to 9, running 10 times in total and filling a tilemap row 10 tiles across.


Click ▶ to see a row of Bubble sprites appear across the top of the screen.

steps.hints: ❓Did you drag the (column) variable into the col parameter of the [place sprite on top of] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓How is the (column) variable used in the [for (column)] loop? 

❓How does the (column) variable change each time the [for (column)] loop is run?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 To generate a variable bubble or rename a variable, tell the ninja that they can right click on the [set [variable] to] block or variable bubble, then select the variable name they’d like to use.

💡Each time the [for (column)]  loop is run, it will increase the (column) variable by 1, as it counts from 0 to 9. Each time the (column) value increases, it places the Bubble sprite 1 column to the right.
steps.instructions:
Name the (index) variable to make it easier to use in the code!


Make a variable named column and drag the [set [column] to] block inside the [function createBubbles] container, at the top. In the [for index] loop, right click (index) to change it to (column). Then, replace (index) with (column) in the [place sprite on top of] block.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you drag the entire [for (column)] loop inside the [for (row)] loop and set the loop to run from 0 to 5?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓What happens when the nested loops run when the [createBubbles] function is called?

❓Does it matter in which order (of nesting) the [for (row)] and [for (column)] loops are placed?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡When the [createBubbles] function is run, 6 rows of 10 Bubble sprites appear on the screen. The nested loops generate multiple rows by iterating through the inner [for (column)] loop the number of times specified in the [for (row)] loop. In this case, [for (row)] 0, the [for (column)] loop is run and generates 10 Bubble sprites in 1 row; [for (row)] 1, the [for (column)] loop is run and generates 10 Bubble sprites in 1 row, and so on.

💡In this example, it does not necessarily matter which loop is the outer and which is the inner; it will just impact the placement of the Bubble sprites. For instance, if reversed, the program would place 6 Bubble sprites in 1 column first, then move to the next column, instead of placing them by rows.
steps.instructions:
Create multiple rows of Bubble sprites!


Drag a second [for index] loop inside the [function createBubbles] container, and set the loop to run from 0 to 5, to create 6 rows of Bubble sprites. Create a variable named row under the [set column to] block inside the function container, then right click (index) in the new [for index] loop to replace it with a (row) variable. 


Drag the entire [for (column)] loop inside the [for (row)] loop. A loop within a loop is called a nested loop. The “outside loop” will run the “inside loop” the number of times set, over and over, until the “outside loop” is completed. 


Drag a (row) bubble into the row parameter of the [place sprite on top of] block.


Click ▶ to see 6 rows of Bubble sprites appear!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use (pick random) blocks in the vx and vy parameters of the [set sprite velocity to] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓What happens when the Marble sprite hits the Paddle sprite? How does its velocity change?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡When the Marble sprite hits the Paddle sprite, random vx and vy values will be selected, causing the Marble to move in a new direction and at a new speed, each time the event occurs.
steps.instructions:
Set the Marble sprite to move when it hits the Paddle sprite!


Drag a [set sprite velocity to] block inside the [on (Marble) overlaps (Paddle)] container. Replace (mySprite) with the (sprite) bubble. 


Drag a (pick random) block into the vx and vy parameters of the [set sprite velocity to] block. Use -50 and 50 as the vx values, and -150 and -50 as the vy values that the Marble sprite’s speed and direction will randomly be selected between. 


Click ▶ to see the Marble sprite move around the screen!

steps.hints: ❓Did you replace (mySprite) with the (otherSprite) bubble in the [destroy sprite] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓What else might happen when the Marble sprite overlaps with a Bubble sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to reflect on game design to think about what might make the game more engaging, when the Marble sprite overlaps a Bubble sprite.
steps.instructions:
Code the Bubble sprites to pop when the Marble sprite overlaps with them!


Drag a [destroy sprite] block inside the [on (Marble) overlaps (Bubble)] container. Replace (mySprite) with the (otherSprite) bubble. Choose an effect and set the time limit.


Click ▶ to see the Bubble sprites disappear as the Marble sprite overlaps them.

steps.hints: ❓Did you select the Marble sprite name and [bottom] as the direction in the <is sprite hitting wall> block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What event will cause a life to be lost?

❓Why is it important to place this [if then] conditional inside a [forever] loop? What would happen if you placed it in the [on start] container?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider when the [forever] loop runs. Because it runs continuously as the project is used, it is constantly checking to see whether the Marble sprite has hit the floor. If it were placed in the [on start] container, it would only check if the Marble sprite is hitting the floor at the beginning of the project.
steps.instructions:
Lose a life if the Marble sprite hits the floor! 


Drag an [if then] conditional into the [forever] loop. Replace the <true> value with an <is sprite hitting wall> block. Select the Marble sprite’s name and [bottom] as the direction. 


Inside the [if then] conditional, add a [change life by] and [play sound] block. Choose a sound that will let users know they’ve lost a life.


Click ▶ to see the Marble sprite lose a life if it touches the floor!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use a <0=0> comparison block to check the length of the (array of sprites of kind (Bubble))?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Which sprite kind should be selected in the (array of sprites of kind) bubble?

❓ What else might be added to make the game easier or harder to play?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Make sure the ninja has selected the Bubble sprite kind in the (array of sprites of kind) bubble.
steps.instructions:
End the game if all the Bubble sprites have been popped! 


Drag a second [if then] conditional into the [forever] loop. Replace the <true> value with a <0=0> comparison block to check if the (length of array) of the (array of sprites of kind (Bubble)) equals 0. 


Add a [game over] block with a [use effect] block inside the [if then] conditional.


Click ▶ to see the game end when all Bubble sprites have been destroyed.

steps.hints: ❓Did you add customizations to your project, such as dialog boxes, splash screens, or effects?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions might help a user understand how to play the game?

❓What other effects might be added to make the game more exciting to play?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Make the project more engaging by adding directions with a dialog box, changing the background color, and updating any sound effects.


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses a nested [for index] loop to create multiple rows of sprites.

validationItems.text: Create a single row of Bubble sprites across the top of the screen.
Create a new variable to replace the loop’s index variable.
Use a nested loop to create multiple rows of Bubble sprites.

validationItems.text: Marble sprite’s velocity changes when it overlaps the Paddle sprite.
Bubble sprites are destroyed when they are overlapped by the Marble sprite.
Lose a life if the Marble sprite hits the floor.
End the game when all the bubble sprites are destroyed.
Game instructions are shared in a dialog box. Background color and sound effects are added to the game.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 3 of Green Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about [for index] and [while] loops. These loops can be used to control the placement of sprites on a tilemap and make something happen while a certain condition is true. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 3:

badges.title: Around and Around
badges.description: Use advanced loops that offer more control options to repeat code in a project.

badges.title: Card Catalog
badges.description: Use a loop that counts from 0 to a given number to repeat a section of code.

badges.title: Waiting for Things to Change
badges.description: Use a loop that will repeat a section of code while a condition is true.
